think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 24-year-old immigrant from Mexico presents with three weeks of worsening headaches, acute nausea, vomiting, increasing forgetfulness, and acute obstructive hydrocephalus at the level of the posterior third ventricle. An obstructing intraventricular mass causing acute hydrocephalus in a young adult is typically suspected to be a colloid cyst, pineal region tumor, or ependymoma rather than a migrating intraventricular parasitic cyst.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs in the emergency department following neurological evaluation and initial non-contrast head CT demonstrating ventriculomegaly and posterior third ventricle obstruction, immediately prior to urgent external ventricular drain placement, subsequent brain MRI, stereotactic resection, and histopathology.
3. Differential Distinctions: Colloid cyst of the third ventricle was considered as a classic cause of position-dependent headache, vomiting, and acute hydrocephalus, but colloid cysts typically arise in the anterior third ventricle at the foramen of Monro, whereas this lesion obstructed the posterior third ventricle and contained parasitic scolex structures. Primary migraine or benign headache was excluded by persistent progression, new cognitive dysfunction, and acute obstructive ventriculomegaly on CT. Histopathology identifying larval cuticle, suckers, and rostellar hooklets established neurocysticercosis.
case_prompt:
A 24-year-old man presented with a three-week history of headaches that had previously provided partial relief with ibuprofen and acetaminophen. On the day prior to admission, he developed a severe headache accompanied by nausea and multiple bouts of emesis. His mother noted increasing forgetfulness over recent days, and on the day of presentation he experienced general malaise. He denied photophobia, prior history of migraines, or recent sick contacts. He had emigrated from Mexico one year prior to presentation, and there was no family history of headaches or migraines.

On physical examination, the patient was alert and oriented. Cranial nerves II through XII were intact, and vision was grossly intact.

An emergency non-contrast head computed tomography (CT) scan demonstrated ventriculomegaly indicative of obstructive hydrocephalus, with an obstruction in the posterior third ventricle and an atypical appearance in the third ventricle region.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Colloid Cyst of the Third Ventricle / Intraventricular Neoplasm
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered as a classic cause of paroxysmal headache, emesis, and acute obstructive hydrocephalus in young adults, but typically occurs at the anterior foramen of Monro rather than the posterior third ventricle, and surgical histopathology demonstrated a parasitic larval wall rather than a mucinous cyst.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Initial head CT obtained in the ER to evaluate for headache showed ventriculomegaly suggestive of obstructive hydrocephalus with obstruction in the posterior third ventricle and an atypical appearance in the third ventricle region (Figure 1).

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered given initial partial analgesic responsiveness, but excluded by progressive cognitive decline (forgetfulness), lack of personal or family headache history, and neuroimaging revealing obstructive ventriculomegaly.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: He denied history of migraine or recent sick contacts. He emigrated from Mexico one year prior to presentation. There was no family history of migraine or headaches.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Emergent external ventricular drainage and subsequent stereotactic transcortical excision of the third ventricular cyst revealed characteristic cestode larval morphology with a three-layered cuticle, suckers, and rostellum containing hooklets.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Pathology findings showed portions of a cyst wall with an outer cuticle, middle cellular layer, and innermost reticular layer. The cyst contains larval stage of parasite showing gut and scolex with muscular suckers and rostellum containing hooklets, suggestive of neurocysticercosis.

editor_comments: Case distilled to emergency department triage and initial CT findings. Histopathology and surgical excision confined to diagnostic reasoning.
